ANU is a research-intensive, Group of Eight university based in Australia's capital, and international students in this program study alongside a large Canberra-based policy, research and public-service community.
curriculum:
The Master of Business Administration requires completion of 48 units which must consist of:
MGMT8101
- Complexity, Judgement and Decision-Making (3 units)
MGMT8102
- Evidence-Based Practice (3 units)
MGMT8103
- Future Analysis (3 units)
MGMT8104
- Responsible Stewardship and Integrity (3 units)
MGMT8105
- Purpose and Strategic Performance (3 units)
MGMT8106
- Public Sector Resources Management (3 units)
MGMT8107
- Program Implementation and Management (3 units)
MGMT8108
- Organisational Learning and Change (3 units)
MGMT8109
- Leading for High Performance and Resilience (3 units)
MGMT8110
- Communication and Influence (3 units)
MGMT8111
- Innovation in the Public Sector (3 units)
MGMT8112
- Business Skills for the Public Sector Ecosystem (3 units)
MGMT8113
- Internal Consulting Capstone (12 units)
admission_requirements:
Applicants must:
be Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander people, Sir Roland Wilson Foundation Pat Turner Scholars, eligible ANU staff or professionals funded by their employers or other sponsor organisations
and
have a minimum of 5 years of documented professional experience in a managerial role(s)
and have one of the following qualifications:
A Bachelor degree or international equivalent in a cognate discipline with a minimum GPA of 5.0/7.0; or
A Bachelor (Honours) degree or international equivalent in a cognate discipline with a minimum GPA of 5.0/7.0; or
A Graduate Certificate or international equivalent in a cognate discipline with a minimum GPA of 5.0/7.0; or
A Graduate Diploma or international equivalent in a cognate discipline with a minimum GPA of 5.0/7.0; or
A Master degree or international equivalent in a cognate discipline with a minimum GPA of 5.0/7.0; or
48 units of postgraduate courses in a cognate discipline with a minimum GPA of 5.0/7.0; or
GMAT (Graduate Management Admission Test), completed no more than 5 years before the time of application, with a minimum score of 550 (minimum 5.0 in Analytical Writing) and a minimum total of 8 years of full-time equivalent years of professional experience at
ANZSCO Skill Level 1
in a field related to the program; or
GRE General test, completed no more than 5 years before the time of application, with a minimum score of 155 for Verbal Reasoning, 155 for Quantitative Reasoning and 4.0 in Analytical Writing, and a minimum total of 8 years of full-time equivalent years of professional experience at
ANZSCO Skill Level 1
in a field related to the program; or
A minimum total of 15 years of full-time equivalent years of professional experience at
ANZSCO Skill Level 1
in a field related to the program.
The GPA for a Bachelor program will be calculated from (i) a completed Bachelor degree using all grades and/or (ii) a completed Bachelor degree using all grades other than those from the last semester (or equivalent study period) of the Bachelor degree. The higher of the two calculations will be used as the basis for admission.
Ranking and English Language Proficiency:
At a minimum, all applicants must meet program-specific academic/non-academic requirements, and English language requirements. Admission to most ANU programs is on a competitive basis. Therefore, meeting all admission requirements does not automatically guarantee entry.
Diversity factors:
As Australia’s national university, ANU is a global representative of Australian research and education. ANU endeavours to recruit and maintain a diverse and deliberate student cohort representative not only of Australia, but the world. In order to achieve these outcomes, competitive ranking of applicants may be adjusted to ensure access to ANU is a reality for brilliant students from countries across the globe.
Assessment of qualifications:
Unless otherwise indicated, ANU will accept all Australian Qualifications Framework (AQF) qualifications or international equivalents that meet or exceed the published admission requirements of our programs, provided all other admission requirements are also met.
Where an applicant has more than one completed tertiary qualification, ANU will base assessment on the qualification that best meets the admission requirements for the program. Find out more about the Australian Qualifications Framework:
www.aqf.edu.au
.
Unless otherwise indicated, where an applicant has more than one completed tertiary qualification, ANU will calculate the GPA for each qualification separately. ANU will base assessment on the best GPA of all completed tertiary qualifications of the same level or higher.
ANU uses a 7-point Grade Point Average (GPA) scale. All qualifications submitted for admission at ANU will be converted to this common scale, which will determine if an applicant meets our published admission requirements. Find out more about how a 7-point GPA is calculated for Australian universities:
www.uac.edu.au/future-applicants/admission-criteria/tertiary-qualifications
.
In addition, all applicants must provide a completed ANU
MBA Program CV template
containing:
Responses to application questions;
Curriculum vitae clearly identifying periods of full-time and part-time employment experience;
Names and contact details of two professional referees who can verify the experience.
The Master of Business Administration program is highly competitive and has a limit on the number of enrolments in each academic year. Applicants will be initially assessed on the minimum criteria detailed above. Where an applicant meets the minimum criteria, they will then also be ranked based on the merit of their relative work experience, academic and/or GMAT/GRE results.
english_requirements: IELTS Academic Overall 6.5, with no band below 6.0.

Additional information for prospective students
Applications must be received by the 30th September in order to be considered.
Applicants with qualifications obtained outside Australia must have a formal degree equivalency assessment completed by the Australian Psychological Society before submitting an application for study.
Additional factors considered in assessing applications are previous relevant experience, availability of supervision for research component and written application.
Competitive applicants may be invited to participate in a suitability assessment process which will include a panel interview and other activities. Full details will be available on the School of Medicine and Psychology website.
Due to the highly structured nature of this program, it is highly recommended that this program should be taken full-time. name: Master of International Relations
description:
The Coral Bell School's Master of International Relations bills itself, not unreasonably, as the only IR program in Australia that combines mainstream IR theory with sustained regional focus on the Asia-Pacific. That's a distinction that matters if a student's actual interest is China-Australia relations, Pacific Islands security, or Southeast Asian political economy rather than a generic transatlantic-flavoured IR degree imported wholesale from a US or UK textbook tradition.

Structurally it's a 96-unit, two-year program: two foundational courses, two compulsory courses, four core courses, then eight units' worth of electives drawn from a wide list across the Bell School and the broader College of Asia and the Pacific. That elective breadth means two students can graduate with quite different transcripts: one weighted toward security studies, another toward international political economy or diplomacy.

The internship pipeline is the standout practical feature: competitive, credit-bearing placements with NGOs, Australian government departments, embassies, and the private sector, on top of ANU's usual proximity advantage of having DFAT, Defence, and most foreign missions within a short drive of campus.
curriculum:
Foundational courses (2): core IR theory and methods
Compulsory courses (2): required departmental units
Core courses (4): selected from IR-specific offerings covering security, political economy, and regional studies
Electives (8): drawn from Coral Bell School and College of Asia and Pacific offerings, including credit-bearing internship option (subject to competitive application)
Total: 96 units over two years full-time, part-time available
admission_requirements: Bachelor degree, minimum GPA 5.0/7.0 or equivalent

admission_requirements:
Applicants must present one of the following:
Bachelor or international equivalent with GPA 5/7; or
Bachelor or international equivalent with GPA 4/7 and a minimum of 3 years full-time equivalent work experience at ANZSCO Skill Level 1 in a field related to the program; or
Bachelor or international equivalent with GPA 4/7 and a GC or international equivalent with a GPA of 4/7; or
Graduate Diploma or international equivalent with a GPA 4/7; or
48 units of courses in a postgraduate program with a GPA of 4/7; or
Graduate Certificate or international equivalent with a GPA of 4/7 and a minimum of 3 years full-time equivalent work experience at ANZSCO Skill Level 1 in a field related to the program; or
Graduate Records Examination (GRE) General test, completed no more than 5 years before the time of application, with a minimum score of 155 for Verbal Reasoning, 155 for Quantitative Reasoning and 4.0 in Analytical Writing and a minimum of 3 years full-time equivalent work experience at ANZSCO Skill Level 1 in a field related to the program; or
A minimum of 10 years full-time equivalent work experience at ANZSCO Skill Level 1 in a field related to the program.
The GPA for a Bachelor program will be calculated from (i) a completed Bachelor degree using all grades and/or (ii) a completed Bachelor degree using all grades other than those from the last semester (or equivalent study period) of the Bachelor degree. The higher of the two calculations will be used as the basis for admission.
Ranking and English Proficiency:
At a minimum, all applicants must meet program-specific academic/non-academic requirements, and English language requirements. Admission to most ANU programs is on a competitive basis. Therefore, meeting all admission requirements does not automatically guarantee entry.
In line with the University's admissions policy and strategic plan, an assessment for admission may include competitively ranking applicants on the basis of specific academic achievement, English language proficiency and diversity factors. Applicants will first be ranked on a GPA ('GPA1') that is calculated using all but the last semester (or equivalent) of the Bachelor degree used for admission purposes. If required, ranking may further be confirmed on the basis of:
a GPA ('GPA2') calculated on the penultimate and antepenultimate semesters (or equivalent) of the Bachelor degree used for admission purposes; and/or
demonstrating higher-level English language proficiency
Prior to enrolment in this ANU program, all students who gain entry will have their Bachelor degree reassessed, to confirm minimum requirements were met.
Further information:
English language admission requirements and post-admission support
Diversity factors:
As Australia’s national university, ANU is global representative of Australian research and education. ANU endeavours to recruit and maintain a diverse and deliberate student cohort representative not only of Australia, but the world. In order to achieve these outcomes, competitive ranking of applicants may be adjusted to ensure access to ANU is a reality for brilliant students from countries across the globe.
Assessment of qualifications:
Unless otherwise indicated, ANU will accept all Australian Qualifications Framework (AQF) qualifications or international equivalents that meet or exceed the published admission requirements of our programs, provided all other admission requirements are also met.
Where an applicant has more than one completed tertiary qualification, ANU will base assessment on the qualification that best meets the admission requirements for the program. Find out more about the Australian Qualifications Framework:
www.aqf.edu.au
.
Unless otherwise indicated, where an applicant has more than one completed tertiary qualification, ANU will calculate the GPA for each qualification separately. ANU will base assessment on the best GPA of all completed tertiary qualifications of the same level or higher.
ANU uses a 7-point Grade Point Average (GPA) scale. All qualifications submitted for admission at ANU will be converted to this common scale, which will determine if an applicant meets our published admission requirements. Find out more about how a 7-point GPA is calculated for Australian universities:
www.uac.edu.au/future-applicants/admission-criteria/tertiary-qualifications
.

name: Master of Peace and Conflict Studies (Advanced)
description: The Master of Peace and Conflict Studies at the Australian National University equips students with the knowledge and skills to understand the nature of peace and conflict, the causes and experiences of violence, and the ways national and international bodies can respond. The program brings together diverse disciplinary insights, demonstrating how different interpretations of peace and conflict influence what we see and how we judge success and failure. Drawing particularly on the Asia-Pacific but with a global outlook, it prepares graduates to work across private, civil society and governmental organisations. The Advanced version adds a substantial independent research component.
discontinued_note: Appears to correspond to ANU's current (non-Advanced) Master of Peace and Conflict Studies.

English Language Requirements for Admission
Diversity factors:
As Australia’s national university, ANU is global representative of Australian research and education. ANU endeavours to recruit and maintain a diverse and deliberate student cohort representative not only of Australia, but the world. Assessment of qualifications:
Unless otherwise indicated, ANU will accept all Australian Qualifications Framework (AQF) qualifications or international equivalents that meet or exceed the published admission requirements of our programs, provided all other admission requirements are also met.

.
Unless otherwise indicated, where an applicant has more than one completed tertiary qualification, ANU will calculate the GPA for each qualification separately. ANU will base assessment on the best GPA of all completed tertiary qualifications of the same level or higher.
ANU uses a 7-point Grade Point Average (GPA) scale. All qualifications submitted for admission at ANU will be converted to this common scale, which will determine if an applicant meets our published admission requirements. Find out more about how a 7-point GPA is calculated for Australian universities:
www.uac.edu.au/future-applicants/admission-criteria/tertiary-qualifications
.

name: Master of Public Policy
description:
Crawford School rebuilt its Master of Public Policy in 2015 from a one-year program into a two-year, 16-course structure, a deliberate lengthening that reflects Crawford's argument that a serious policy degree needs more than a single accelerated year, especially for the specialisation tracks it now offers. It sits inside the College of Asia and the Pacific, so the program carries a heavier Asia-Pacific and development-economics flavour than an MPP from, say, a Melbourne or Sydney school built around domestic Australian policy.

Students choose between a general MPP or one of several named specialisations: Contemporary Regulation, Economic Policy, Social Research Methods, and Regulation: National and International Regimes among them. The Contemporary Regulation specialisation is a genuine point of difference: compulsory foundation courses in regulatory theory followed by electives that range into disruptive technology regulation, global business regulation, restorative justice, and climate and health policy, an unusually wide net for what's often a narrower regulation label elsewhere.

Since 2024 all Crawford graduate courses run with both in-person and online options, though live attendance at scheduled sessions is still expected. That's useful for the significant share of MPP students who are current or former public servants studying while working, including a steady contingent of students sponsored by governments across the Asia-Pacific region.
curriculum:
Pre-sessional components: quantitative and policy-analysis foundations before formal coursework begins
Year 1: Public Policy foundations, Microeconomics for Policy, Policy Analysis and Program Evaluation, specialisation foundation courses (if pursuing a named specialisation)
Year 2: Specialisation electives (Contemporary Regulation, Economic Policy, Social Research Methods, or International Regimes), capstone policy project, general electives
Total: 16 courses over two years; general MPP or named specialisation pathway available; in-person or online delivery with scheduled live sessions
admission_requirements: Bachelor degree GPA 4.0/7.0 plus 3 years relevant work experience, or equivalent
english_requirements: IELTS 6.5 (no band below 6.0) or equivalent

description: The Master of Science in Astronomy and Astrophysics is a graduate program at the Australian National University in Canberra, run through the ANU College of Science and Medicine, taken over 2 years full-time (96 Units). Coursework includes a minimum of 72 units from completion of courses from the lists below. Graduates are expected to demonstrate high level knowledge in astronomy and astrophysics and relate it to a range of disciplinary and interdisciplinary contexts. A minimum of 24 units must come from completion of 8000-level courses.

A minimum of 72 units from completion of courses from the lists below:

admission_requirements:
Applicants must present a Bachelor degree or international equivalent
with a minimum GPA of at least 5.0/7.0
with at least 8 courses in a cognate discipline, which must also have a minimum GPA of 5.0/7.0.
with a minimum of 2 courses of undergraduate second year Physics; and a minimum of 1 course of undergraduate second year Mathematics.
The GPA requirement for this program must be met by both the program as a whole, as well as by the 8 courses in a cognate discipline. Where more than 8 cognate courses have been completed by the applicant, ANU will take the best 8 courses when assessing the cognate GPA.
The GPA for a Bachelor program will be calculated from (i) a completed Bachelor degree using all grades and/or (ii) a completed Bachelor degree using all grades other than those from the last semester (or equivalent study period) of the Bachelor degree. The higher of the two calculations will be used as the basis for admission.
Additional admission information:
Students applying for this program will need to have a background in physics equivalent to undergraduate second year quantum mechanics, statistical mechanics, and electromagnetism in order to meet prerequisites for many of the ASTR- and PHYS- courses listed in this program. They will also need to have a background in Mathematics, equivalent at least to the level of ANU
MATH2305
.
Ranking and English language proficiency:
At a minimum, all applicants must meet program-specific academic/non-academic requirements, and English language requirements. Admission to most ANU programs is on a competitive basis. Therefore, meeting all admission requirements does not automatically guarantee entry. In line with the University's admissions policy and strategic plan, an assessment for admission may include competitively ranking applicants on the basis of specific academic achievement, English language proficiency and diversity factors. Applicants will first be ranked on a GPA ('GPA1') that is calculated using all but the last semester (or equivalent) of the Bachelor degree used for admission purposes. If required, ranking may further be confirmed on the basis of:
a GPA ('GPA2') calculated on the penultimate and antepenultimate semesters (or equivalent) of the Bachelor degree used for admission purposes; and/or
demonstrating higher-level English language proficiency
Prior to enrolment in this ANU program, all students who gain entry will have their Bachelor degree reassessed, to confirm minimum requirements were met.
Further information:
English language admission requirements and post-admission support
Diversity factors:
As Australia’s national university, ANU is global representative of Australian research and education. ANU endeavours to recruit and maintain a diverse and deliberate student cohort representative not only of Australia, but the world. In order to achieve these outcomes, competitive ranking of applicants may be adjusted to ensure access to ANU is a reality for brilliant students from countries across the globe.
Assessment of qualifications:
Unless otherwise indicated, ANU will accept all Australian Qualifications Framework (AQF) qualifications or international equivalents that meet or exceed the published admission requirements of our programs, provided all other admission requirements are also met.
Where an applicant has more than one completed tertiary qualification, ANU will base assessment on the qualification that best meets the admission requirements for the program. Find out more about the Australian Qualifications Framework:
www.aqf.edu.au
.
Unless otherwise indicated, where an applicant has more than one completed tertiary qualification, ANU will calculate the GPA for each qualification separately. ANU will base assessment on the best GPA of all completed tertiary qualifications of the same level or higher.
ANU uses a 7-point Grade Point Average (GPA) scale. All qualifications submitted for admission at ANU will be converted to this common scale, which will determine if an applicant meets our published admission requirements. Find out more about how a 7-point GPA is calculated for Australian universities:
www.uac.edu.au/future-applicants/admission-criteria/tertiary-qualifications

name: Bachelor of Arts
description:
Avondale's Bachelor of Arts covers more scientific ground than the name implies. Biological Science, Chemistry and Mathematics all sit as available majors alongside the humanities staples (English, History, Music, Communication, Religious Studies), a structural quirk that comes from Avondale folding its science majors into the BA rather than running them exclusively through the Bachelor of Science. Students pick an 8-unit major and can add a 4-unit minor from the same list, or take strands borrowed from Business or Ministry and Theology to build a more interdisciplinary profile.

The Communication major is the one with a defined career on-ramp built into the structure: it requires a professional internship in the final year, placing students with media, marketing, or communications employers rather than leaving that experience to chance. Chaplaincy is the other major with embedded work-integrated learning, reflecting Avondale's role training pastoral and chaplaincy staff for Adventist schools and hospitals across the region.
curriculum:
24 units, 144 credit points, three years full-time
Major (8 units) chosen from: Biological Science, Chaplaincy, Chemistry, Communication, English, Food & Nutrition, History, Mathematics, Music, Religious Studies, Visual Arts
Optional minor (4 units) from the same list, or a strand from Business or Ministry & Theology
Christian Studies core units
Communication major: Professional Internship unit in final year
Chaplaincy major: work-integrated learning embedded across CHPL-coded units
General elective units to complete the 24-unit total
admission_requirements: Year 12 completion or equivalent
english_requirements: IELTS 6.5 (no band below 6.0) or equivalent

name: Bachelor of Arts/Bachelor of Teaching (Secondary)
description:
This is Avondale's combined arts/teaching degree for people who know from day one they want to teach secondary school. It runs longer than the standalone BA (the paired BSc/BTeaching runs 32 units over four years, and this Arts equivalent follows a similar extended structure) because it has to satisfy both a full arts major and NSW Education Standards Authority accreditation requirements for secondary teaching in that subject area.

Graduates come out with two teaching methods areas typically drawn from English, History, Music, or Religious Studies, which matters practically: secondary schools, and especially the Adventist school system Avondale feeds heavily into, hire teachers who can cover two subjects on a timetable, not one. Professional experience placements are substantial and staged across the degree, from early observation placements in first year building up to a full practicum block in final year, rather than concentrated into a single end-of-course prac.
curriculum:
Combined BA content major (8 units) plus a second teaching method area, drawn from English, History, Music, or Religious Studies
Education core: Educational Psychology, Curriculum and Pedagogy, Classroom Management, Assessment and Reporting
Professional experience placements staged from Year 1 observation through to a capstone full-time practicum block in final year
NSW Education Standards Authority (NESA)-accredited secondary teaching methods units
Christian Studies core units
Final-year Professional Studies seminar preparing for graduate teacher accreditation
admission_requirements: Year 12 completion or equivalent
english_requirements: IELTS 7.5 (no band below 7.0) or equivalent (teaching registration requirement)

name: Bachelor of Business
description:
The Bachelor of Business at Avondale is a 24-unit degree structured around double majors rather than a single specialisation. Most students pair accounting with a second area (marketing, HR, or business administration) or take a major-and-minor combination, and the accounting major itself carries accreditation from both CPA Australia and Chartered Accountants ANZ, which matters if the end goal is a CA or CPA designation later.

The smaller cohort size compared to a metropolitan business school shows up in practice: internship placements are built into the course rather than bolted on as an optional extra, and Avondale's business faculty draws on its Sydney campus location (Wahroonga) for placements with businesses and Adventist-affiliated organisations across Sydney's north. Christian Studies core units run alongside the standard business core, including accounting, economics, management, marketing, and law, reflecting the university's integration of faith and vocation rather than treating them as separate tracks.
curriculum:
Business core (Years 1–2): Financial Accounting, Economics, Marketing Principles, Business Law, Management, Business Statistics, Business Communication
Major 1 and Major 2 (or major + minor), selected from Accounting, Marketing, Human Resource Management, Business Administration, with an Entrepreneurship minor available
Christian Studies core units (compulsory across all Avondale undergraduate degrees)
Professional internship unit, undertaken within a major or minor field of study
Capstone: Strategic Management or equivalent integrative unit in final semester
Elective units to complete 144 credit points across 24 units
admission_requirements: Year 12 completion or equivalent
english_requirements: IELTS 6.5 (no band below 6.0) or equivalent

name: Bachelor of Nursing
description:
Nursing is arguably the program Avondale is best known for outside its own denomination, largely because of the pipeline into Sydney Adventist Hospital ('the San') and other major health networks across the Hunter and Central Coast region. The course runs 24 units over six full-time semesters and builds in more clinical hours than the accreditation minimum: students log at least 800 hours of professional experience placement, starting from semester two once first-year prerequisites and pre-clinical checks (police check, vaccination status, National Police Certificate) are cleared.

What distinguishes the Avondale version from a standard metropolitan nursing degree is the deliberate inclusion of a whole-person model of care, a legacy of the university's Seventh-day Adventist health philosophy, which has produced a genuine research output in lifestyle medicine and preventive health (the same tradition behind the Blue Zones research on Adventist longevity in Loma Linda, California, that Avondale's own academics have contributed to). Clinical rotations cover acute medical/surgical wards, emergency and ICU exposure, maternal and child health, mental health, aged care and community settings, so graduates aren't narrowly trained into one specialty before they've even sat the registration exam.
curriculum:
Year 1: Foundations of Nursing Practice, Anatomy & Physiology I & II, Introduction to Professional Nursing, Psychology for Health Professionals
Year 1 Semester 2: first clinical placement block begins (subject to pre-clinical clearance)
Year 2: Medical-Surgical Nursing, Mental Health Nursing, Pathophysiology & Pharmacology, Research in Nursing Practice, extended clinical placements in acute and high-dependency settings
Year 3: Maternal & Child Health Nursing, Aged Care and Chronic Disease Management, Community and Primary Health Care Nursing, Emergency and Critical Care Nursing, capstone Transition to Professional Practice placement
Minimum 800 hours supervised clinical placement across acute, community, mental health and aged care settings
Registration pathway: eligible for AHPRA registration as a Registered Nurse on graduation
admission_requirements: Year 12 completion or equivalent
english_requirements: IELTS 7.0 (no band below 6.5) or equivalent

name: Bachelor of Science
description:
The standalone Bachelor of Science at Avondale is smaller than its BA counterpart in terms of enrolments, since several of the science disciplines (Biological Science, Chemistry, Food & Nutrition, Mathematics) are also offered as majors within the Bachelor of Arts. Students choosing the BS specifically want the science degree title, often because it reads better for graduate entry into health science postgraduate courses, dietetics, or laboratory-based careers.

Food & Nutrition is worth flagging as a genuine point of difference: it draws on Avondale's Adventist health heritage (the same institutional lineage that produced Sanitarium and its Weet-Bix brand a century ago) and is taught with a research base in lifestyle and preventive health rather than as a generic nutrition science unit bolted onto a chemistry-heavy degree. Students combining it with Biological Science are well placed for further study in dietetics or public health.
curriculum:
Major (8 units) chosen from Biological Science, Chemistry, Food & Nutrition, or Mathematics
Core mathematics and science foundation units in Year 1
Second major or 4-unit minor from the same disciplines
Laboratory-based practical units across chemistry and biological science majors
Christian Studies core units
Research or research-methods unit in final year for students proceeding to honours or postgraduate study
24 units, 144 credit points, three years full-time
admission_requirements: Year 12 completion or equivalent
english_requirements: IELTS 6.5 (no band below 6.0) or equivalent

name: Bachelor of Theology
description:
Avondale runs one of the only standalone Bachelor of Theology degrees in Australia housed within a Seventh-day Adventist institution, and the course reflects that heritage directly: alongside standard biblical studies and biblical languages (Greek and Hebrew feature prominently), students work through Adventist doctrinal history and the denomination's distinctive eschatology, taught by faculty attached to the Seminary at the Cooranbong campus.

Most students aren't just doing this for personal interest. A large share go on to ministerial credentialing within the Adventist Church across Australia and the Pacific, or use the degree as the entry point into postgraduate theological study (Avondale's own Master of Arts in Theology, or seminaries overseas). The course is unapologetically confessional rather than comparative-religion in orientation, which is worth knowing going in: this isn't a general religious studies degree, it's training within a specific tradition.
curriculum:
24 units, 144 credit points, six full-time semesters
Biblical Studies core: Old Testament Introduction, New Testament Introduction, Biblical Hermeneutics
Biblical languages: Greek I & II, Hebrew I & II
Systematic and Adventist Theology units, including denominational history and eschatology
Christian History and Church History units
Practical/Pastoral units: homiletics (preaching), pastoral care, mission and evangelism
Elective units and a research or ministry-placement capstone in final year
admission_requirements: Year 12 completion or equivalent
english_requirements: IELTS 6.5 (no band below 6.0) or equivalent

name: Master of Arts
description:
Avondale's Master of Arts is a coursework postgraduate degree that mirrors the BA's breadth into postgraduate territory, with a Theology and Religious Studies concentration being the most established pathway given the Seminary's presence on the Cooranbong campus. Students who did their undergraduate degree elsewhere and want to formalise theological study without committing to a full Master of Divinity often land here.

Because cohorts are small, the degree runs with a good deal of supervisory attention per student, and a research project or minor thesis component in the final stage of the degree is standard rather than optional. This isn't a pure coursework-only credential; it expects candidates to produce a piece of independent research under supervision by the end.
curriculum:
Coursework units in the chosen discipline (e.g. Theology, Religious Studies, English, History)
Research Methods unit (compulsory)
Advanced seminar units in the specialisation area
Minor thesis or research project, undertaken in the final stage under individual supervision
Elective units to complete the total credit point requirement for the degree

english_requirements: IELTS 6.5 (no band below 6.0) or equivalent

name: Master of Education
description:
Avondale's Master of Education is built for working teachers rather than career-changers. Every unit runs by distance, with a single Winter School each July drawing students back to the Lake Macquarie campus for a week of face-to-face intensives. That residential week matters more than it sounds: it's where the small cohort (Avondale's education postgrad numbers stay modest compared to the Group of Eight providers) actually meets in person, and where the program's Christian education strand gets taught alongside the research methodology core.

The degree suits teachers chasing a leadership track, a curriculum specialisation, or simply the credential bump for promotion within Adventist and independent school systems, where an Avondale postgrad carries particular weight. Because it's capped at eight units (48 credit points) and deliberately excludes a full-time pathway (Avondale is upfront that some units simply aren't offered often enough to support one), most candidates are two to three years into full-time teaching before they enrol, doing the degree one or two units a semester around a teaching load.

General stream: 4 elective units drawn across multiple specialisation lists for an unspecialised MEd
2 remaining units to complete the 8-unit, 48 credit-point total
Winter School residential (July, Lake Macquarie campus) attached to select units
No capstone thesis in the standard coursework pattern; research-intensive exit available via an extended project unit in some strands

name: Master of Leadership and Management
description:
A 12-unit postgraduate degree aimed at people already in, or heading into, management roles who want the credential without leaving their job. It's delivered by distance with a mid-year residential intensive, which is the only time the cohort is physically together. One compulsory unit, LAMC50600 Theology, Theory and Practice of Leadership, signals the degree's actual orientation: it treats leadership as something with an ethical and, specifically, a Christian dimension, not just a set of management techniques lifted from a generic MBA-style curriculum.

Compared to Avondale's separate Master of Business Administration, this degree sits closer to organisational leadership than finance or strategy: it's a reasonable fit for people running teams in healthcare, education, ministry, or not-for-profit settings where Avondale's networks (particularly Adventist Church institutions across the Pacific) provide a natural graduate destination, though it isn't restricted to those sectors.

name: Master of Nursing (Coursework)
description:
This is Avondale's postgraduate nursing pathway for registered nurses who already hold a first degree and want to specialise rather than start over. At 11 units (72 credit points) it's a lean coursework masters, and it's built with defined exit points: a Graduate Certificate at 4 units, a Graduate Diploma at 8, so a nurse who needs to pause partway through still walks away with a recognised credential rather than nothing.

The two specialisation tracks on offer, Clinical Nursing/Clinical Teaching and Leadership and Management, split off after five shared core units, and the choice matters for career direction: one leads toward advanced clinical practice or clinical education roles (increasingly in demand as hospital-based clinical facilitator positions expand), the other toward nurse unit manager and health service leadership positions. Given Avondale's ties to Sydney Adventist Hospital, a number of students are already working within that network while completing the degree part-time.

name: Bachelor of Actuarial Science
description:
Bond is one of only seven universities in Australia accredited by the Actuaries Institute, and the only one in Queensland, so the Bachelor of Actuarial Science is built to carry students through Part I (Foundation) exemptions rather than leaving that accreditation work for after graduation. The degree runs across three years, with subjects sequenced into connected themes each trimester so probability, financial mathematics and statistical modelling build on each other rather than sitting as isolated units.

International students complete the program across the January and September intakes, giving two full semesters a year rather than Bond's usual three, while domestic students can use all three trimesters to finish faster. Class sizes stay small enough that lecturers know students by name, which matters in a discipline where a misunderstood assumption in one trimester tends to resurface as a mistake two subjects later. Graduates leave with a credential recognised by employers hiring for insurance, superannuation and financial risk roles across Australia.
curriculum:
Trimester 1: Introduction to Probability and Statistics, Financial Mathematics, Microeconomics, Communication and Thought
Trimester 2: Life Contingencies I, Regression Modelling, Macroeconomics, Corporate Finance
Trimester 3: Life Contingencies II, Survival Models, Stochastic Processes, Business Law
Trimester 4: Actuarial Statistics, Investment and Asset Modelling, Financial Reporting, elective
Trimester 5: Actuarial Modelling and Simulation, Risk Theory, Actuarial Control Cycle, elective
Trimester 6: Capstone actuarial project, Professionalism and Ethics for Actuaries, discipline electives
Program maps to Part I (Foundation Program) exemptions with the Actuaries Institute on completion.

name: Bachelor of Biomedical Science
description:
Bond's Bachelor of Biomedical Science is a two-year accelerated degree, made possible by studying across all three of Bond's trimesters rather than the usual two-semester academic year, a genuine time saving for students planning to go on to medicine, physiotherapy or another postgraduate health program where a biomedical degree is the entry pathway rather than the destination.

Students choose between two majors partway through the degree. The Pre-Health/Professional major is aimed at students heading toward clinical postgraduate study, pairing a Health Communication subject with electives chosen from nutrition, exercise and sports science, psychology or health innovation. The Laboratory/Research major instead trains students in advanced bioscience laboratory technique and molecular diagnostics, culminating in a two-semester individual research project, closer to what a student heading into medical research or a PhD would want on transcript. Both majors share a common science core in the first year, so the choice doesn't have to be locked in on day one.

description:

name: Bachelor of Climate Change and Sustainable Action
description:
Bond University's Bachelor of Climate Change and Sustainable Action is deliberately not a climate science degree. It is a two-year non-science degree (six semesters, trimester intakes in January, May, and September) that approaches climate and sustainability through communication, media, psychology, health, law, and business. The structure is a core curriculum, a broad interdisciplinary foundation, a student-chosen major, and an electives and capstone block.

The final semester can be a capstone project or an internship applying the degree to a real sustainability problem, with some fieldwork such as environmental assessments. Graduates move into sustainability management, climate consulting, environmental policy, corporate governance and communications, and infrastructure planning. Students who want the science side (emissions modelling, ecology, engineering) should look at a science or engineering degree instead.

name: Bachelor of Clinical Exercise Physiology
description:
Bond added this degree to replace its Bachelor of Exercise and Sports Science, which stops taking students from January 2027. It runs over seven semesters (two years and four months) and moves from foundational exercise science into clinical practice, covering anatomy, pathophysiology, exercise prescription, behaviour change, biomechanics, and digital health.

Students complete at least 500 hours of supervised clinical placement across rehabilitation, sport, private practice, and community health, weighted toward the final year (roughly 70, 70, 180, and 180 hours across semesters three, four, six, and seven). One caveat for prospective students: as of 2026 the program is not yet accredited by Exercise and Sports Science Australia. Bond has applied and expects a decision in late 2026, aiming for provisional accreditation before the first cohort graduates. Accreditation is what allows graduates to register as Accredited Exercise Physiologists, so applicants should confirm its status before enrolling.

name: Bachelor of Construction Management and Quantity Surveying
description:
A two-year accelerated degree (six semesters) covering construction technology, site management, contract administration, building measurement, tendering and finance, project delivery systems, and risk management. First year pairs introductory construction subjects with Bond's core subjects; second year works through the professional subjects and ends with an industry-based capstone project.

The degree carries a strong set of accreditations: the Australian Institute of Quantity Surveyors, the Chartered Institute of Building, and the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors, and it meets the education requirement for a Queensland Open Builders Licence. name: Bachelor of Design in Architecture
description:
The first stage of Bond's architecture pathway: a two-year studio degree (27 subjects, trimester intakes in January, May, and September) at the Abedian School of Architecture, where each student gets an assigned desk in an open-plan studio. Learning is project-based, with access to computing and fabrication labs, a robotics lab, workshops, 3D printers, large-format laser cutters, CNC routers, and industrial robot arms.

This degree alone does not make someone an architect. Graduates progress to Bond's Master of Architecture (about one year and four months), which is the accredited qualification for registration in Australia and elsewhere, but entry to the master's is by application and not automatic. The program includes work-integrated learning and twice-yearly student exhibitions that build the portfolio.

Bond University's Bachelor of Digital Transformation is a two-year degree (six semesters) that sits between business and technology rather than inside either. It is explicitly not an engineering or computer science degree: the focus is leading change and working alongside AI tools, not building them. Subjects span AI and design thinking, law and technology, cyber security, business statistics, digital literacy, and digital advertising.

name: Bachelor of Health Sciences (Honours, Intensive)
description: The accelerated version of Bond's Bachelor of Health Sciences honours year, completed in two semesters on Bond's three-intake calendar rather than three. It is a research year taken after a bachelor's degree in health sciences or a related field: advanced coursework in research design and methods plus a supervised honours thesis in an area matched to a supervisor. Entry requires a strong grade average in the prior degree. The result is classified, and a good honours classification is the standard entry point to a PhD. It suits health sciences graduates who want to move quickly into research or strengthen their profile for postgraduate study or competitive health programs.
curriculum: Required: Required HLSC41-151: Research Analysis and Communication (Intensive) (15CP) The successful conduct of research requires advanced abilities in analysis and interpretation of data, critical thinking, and written and oral presentation. This subject, along with the skills developed in the subject "Research Preparation & Design", supports Health Sciences Honours students as they progress into their Honours program. A thorough coverage of mathematical and statistical (quantitative) procedures, as well as qualitative approaches, will be provided in order to support both the project design and data analysis. Parametric and non-parametric statistical methods will be examined including t-tests, analysis of variance (ANOVA), correlation, and regression. Workshops will actively develop students' skills in a variety of communication formats including the writing of discipline-specific journal articles, short abstracts, and funding proposals. Students will also participate in regular presentation sessions including oral and poster presentations. Read more . HLSC41-152: Research Preparation and Design (Intensive) (15CP) This subject is designed to provide the framework and skills necessary for Honours students to successfully commence a research project in the Health Sciences. Students will work closely with the Honours convenor and individual project supervisors to develop their research topic, formulate their aims and hypotheses and consider the significance of the project. Workshops will enable students to search for and retrieve, interpret and begin to critically evaluate the relevant literature in their field. Research ethics processes will be discussed and debated, and students will be assisted to complete ethics applications where appropriate for their study. Students will also review various research design strategies and identify appropriate methods for conducting their project and analysing their expected data. Finally

name: Bachelor of Journalism
description:
Bond's Bachelor of Journalism is a two-year degree (six semesters) that can be extended to a bachelor plus master's in three years. First year teaches newsroom reporting, feature writing, content creation, and digital publishing alongside three of Bond's core subjects; second year adds a major or minor chosen from more than 15 options. Students produce podcasts, video packages, television segments, news and magazine articles, and published websites.

The faculty runs a dedicated newsroom, a three-camera television studio, audio suites, and more than 40 editing stations. Internships are arranged with organisations including the ABC, Channel 7, Channel 10, and The Guardian, and Bond runs overseas reporting placements in New York, Washington, Beijing, and London. The portfolio students build across the degree is the main thing they take to employers.

name: Bachelor of Laws
description:
Bond's Faculty of Law caps annual admission at around 180 students specifically to keep classes small, and the Bachelor of Laws uses that scale to run a genuinely accelerated model: eight semesters across Bond's three-trimester calendar, finishing in two years and eight months rather than the three or four years an LLB takes at a standard two-semester university. Students complete 170 credit points across 32 subjects: 17 compulsory law subjects, seven law electives, three university core subjects and five general electives.

The teaching emphasis sits on practice as much as doctrine: legal research and reasoning, legal writing and drafting, oral advocacy, negotiation and dispute resolution, and legal ethics are built into the compulsory sequence rather than left to a single skills subject. Because trimesters run back-to-back with short breaks, students moving straight through need to plan around a genuinely continuous academic year, which suits those wanting to qualify and move into practice or further study as quickly as possible.
curriculum:
Compulsory law subjects (17): Contracts, Torts, Criminal Law, Constitutional Law, Property Law, Equity and Trusts, Administrative Law, Corporations Law, Evidence, Civil Procedure, Legal Ethics and Professional Responsibility, and others across the sequence
Law electives (7 subjects): drawn from areas such as intellectual property, international law, family law, competition law and litigation practice
University core subjects (3): communication, thinking and analysis subjects taken by all Bond undergraduates
General electives (5): open to any faculty, used to add breadth or a minor
Integrated legal skills strand: legal research and writing, oral advocacy, negotiation and dispute resolution embedded across compulsory subjects
Total: 170 credit points / 32 subjects across 8 trimesters (2 years 8 months full-time)

name: Bachelor of Medical Studies
description: Bond University's Bachelor of Medical Studies is the first of two combined degrees that make up the Bond Medical Program, the shortest pathway to becoming a doctor in Australia at four years and eight months across Bond's three-semester year. Direct entry is limited to Australian citizens, permanent residents, Australian Humanitarian visa holders and New Zealand citizens; international students can still reach the program by first completing a recognised Bond pathway degree such as the Bachelor of Biomedical Science. The first two years, known as the preclinical years, are built around small-group, case-based learning, clinical skills laboratories, simulation and community placements, moving through the human lifecycle and body systems while introducing population health, First Nations health and medical ethics. In year three, students relocate to the Bond University Clinical Education and Research Centre at Robina Hospital for a full year of clinical immersion, working through core disciplines including surgery, general practice, internal medicine and emergency medicine before transitioning into the Doctor of Medicine.
curriculum: Years 1-3 (the preclinical years). Year 1 (2 semesters): four integrated domains covering the molecular and cellular foundations of the body's systems, the psychological and population-health basis of human behaviour including First Nations health, foundational clinical and communication skills, and professionalism and medico-legal principles. Year 2 (3 semesters): a second, more complex pass through the body systems covering disease processes, diagnostic investigations and health psychology, with continued clinical-skills and ethics training. Year 3 (3 semesters): core clinical disciplines - surgery, women's health, general practice, internal medicine, child health, mental health and emergency medicine - taught through Bond Virtual Healthcare patient cases and clinical placements based at the Bond University Clinical Education and Research Centre, Robina Hospital, preparing students for the Doctor of Medicine.
admission_requirements: Direct entry is limited to Australian citizens, Australian permanent residents, Australian Humanitarian visa holders and New Zealand citizens. Applicants are assessed on academic result, subject prerequisites (English, English as an Additional Language, Literature, or English & Literature Extension at QCAA Units 3 and 4, Grade C or better, or an equivalent), an interview and psychometric testing. Up to 180 domestic places are offered each year across the May and September intakes, 80% to undergraduate (school-leaver) applicants and 20% to graduate applicants; competitive undergraduate applicants typically present an ATAR of 96 or higher (or IB 38+), while graduate applicants typically present a GPA above 6 on a 7-point scale.
english_requirements: English proficiency is met through the QCAA English, English as an Additional Language, Literature, or English & Literature Extension subject prerequisite (or a recognised equivalent) rather than a separate language test, reflecting the program's domestic-only direct-entry policy for Australian and New Zealand citizens and permanent residents.

name: Bachelor of Policy, Philosophy and Economics
description:
Bond's version of the politics, philosophy and economics degree, built across three faculties (Law, Business, and Society and Design). It runs on three strands: policy and law reform, philosophy and competing worldviews, and the economic analysis of policy, with politics threaded through. First year lays foundations in legal studies, international relations, philosophy, politics, and economics; second year moves into contemporary policy problems, with about five open electives for customisation.

Bond's three-semester calendar lets the standard three-year PPE structure be completed faster. The degree is aimed at students heading into the public service, government, policy institutes, think tanks, and not-for-profits, where the ability to reason across law, economics, and ethics matters more than depth in any one.

name: Bachelor of Project Management
description:
A two-year degree (six semesters) that is unusual as an undergraduate offering, since project management is more often studied at postgraduate level. First year builds business fundamentals and the project framework; second year works through scheduling, budgeting, resourcing, scope, quality, procurement, risk, and stakeholder management using case studies, ending with a capstone in project integration management.

The degree is endorsed by the Australian Institute of Project Management, accredited by the Project Management Institute's Global Accreditation Center, structured around the PMBOK Guide, and also carries Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors accreditation. Students can join Bond's Transformer program for real cross-disciplinary project work. It is aimed at students who want to enter project or program coordination roles directly rather than moving into them from another field.

name: Bachelor of Property
description:
Bond University's Bachelor of Property is a two-year degree (six semesters, 24 subjects) covering the full property cycle: development and feasibility, land economy, valuation, property finance and investment, corporate real estate, urban and sustainable development, property rights and taxation, and spatial information systems. name: Bachelor of Psychological Science
description:
The Bachelor of Psychological Science is accredited with conditions by the Australian Psychology Accreditation Council and approved by the Psychology Board of Australia, and it's built to count as the first three years of the standard six-year pathway to registration as a psychologist. Bond's three-trimester calendar means students can finish the bachelor's component in two years rather than the usual three, and the full run through to a fourth (honours) year and into a master's-level registration pathway can be completed in four years and eight months.

The subject list covers the breadth APAC requires: biological psychology, cognitive psychology, social psychology, personality and learning, developmental psychology, psychopathology, and cross-cultural psychology all appear across the degree rather than being compressed into one or two survey subjects. Graduates who complete the honours year become eligible to apply for provisional registration with AHPRA and move on to a master's program. The degree is explicitly built as a stepping stone rather than a terminal qualification for most students who take it.

Year 1: Introduction to Psychology, Biological Psychology, Research Methods and Statistics I, Developmental Psychology
Year 2: Cognitive Psychology, Social Psychology, Personality, Learning and Behaviour, Research Methods and Statistics II
Upper level: Psychopathology, Motivation and Emotion, Cross-Cultural Psychology, Health Psychology
Final trimester: Applied research project and electives
APAC-accredited (with conditions), PsyBA-approved; equivalent to years 1–3 of the 6-year registration pathway
Optional progression: Bachelor of Psychological Science (Honours), then master's-level registration program

name: Bachelor of Psychological Science (Honours)
description:
This is an eight-month honours year (two semesters), not a full degree, taken after a three-year psychology sequence. Semester one covers multivariate research methods, human experimental psychology, and research ethics; semester two covers psychological assessment and professional practice while students complete a supervised research thesis.

It is accredited by the Australian Psychology Accreditation Council and counts as the fourth year of the six-year pathway to registration as a psychologist, so finishing it makes a graduate eligible to apply for provisional registration with AHPRA and for master's-level clinical programs. Students work from a dedicated fourth-year lab with statistical software and use Bond's cognitive research labs and test library. Entry is competitive and based on grades in the prior psychology major.

description: A pre-university course run by Bond University College for students who have finished school but do not yet meet the academic requirements for direct bachelor entry, including many international students whose qualifications sit below Australian Year 12. It runs about nine to ten months and combines academic subjects with English and study skills, taught in small classes. On completion at the required standard, students progress into the first year of a Bond bachelor's degree. It suits school leavers who need a recognised bridging year before starting an undergraduate degree at Bond.
admission_requirements: Completion of Australian Year 11 (or equivalent secondary schooling); the Foundation Program prepares students for direct entry into a Bond bachelor's degree.
english_requirements: IELTS Overall 5.5, with no band below 5.0 (or equivalent), for entry to the pathway program.

name: Bond-BBT Graduate Certificate in Global Leadership

It is aimed at professionals working in or toward executive roles with a focus on Japan and the wider Asia-Pacific. Because it is online, students who need an Australian student visa cannot enrol. It suits managers who want a short, credentialled introduction to global leadership and a start on the Bond-BBT MBA.

name: Doctor of Legal Science (Research)
description: Bond University's Doctor of Legal Science is a research doctorate in law, the SJD, which differs from a PhD in law by combining structured coursework with a shorter thesis of about 50,000 words. The program runs four years full-time or eight years part-time. Candidates complete up to six postgraduate law electives before starting their independent research, and applicants who already hold a Master of Laws can reduce the coursework in exchange for a longer thesis. The thesis must make a significant contribution to knowledge in an area of law and demonstrate independent scholarship, supervised by a principal and associate supervisors. It suits practising lawyers and legal scholars who want doctoral-level research training with a taught component, rather than the pure-research path of a PhD.
curriculum: Thesis Option: Students must complete a major dissertation (of approximately 50,000 words which represents an original contribution to the knowledge and understanding of an aspect of law and which demonstrates a capacity for independent research. The faculty must approve the topic and appropriate supervision must be available. LAWS99-501: SJD Thesis - Law Read more .
admission_requirements: Applicants must have a Bachelor of Laws (Honours), Juris Doctor (Honours), Master of Laws degree or equivalent.

name: Doctor of Medicine
description: Bond University's Doctor of Medicine is the second, postgraduate stage of the Bond Medical Program, following the Bachelor of Medical Studies to give eligible graduates registration as a medical practitioner in Australia or New Zealand. As with the Bachelor, direct entry is limited to Australian citizens, permanent residents, Australian Humanitarian visa holders and New Zealand citizens; international students can still reach the Doctor of Medicine by first completing a recognised Bond pathway degree such as the Bachelor of Biomedical Science, Master of Occupational Therapy or Doctor of Physiotherapy and meeting the required GPA and prerequisites. Teaching continues the clinical immersion begun in year three of the Bachelor, working through 12 clinical rotations across hospital and community healthcare settings in areas including women's health, child health, mental health, surgery, emergency medicine and general practice, plus a selective and two elective or pre-internship placements in Australia or overseas. Graduates complete a research, professional or capstone project and portfolio, and are eligible for registration as a medical practitioner in any Australian state or territory, or in New Zealand.
curriculum: An Extended Masters (Level 9) program delivered through clinical rotations in hospital and community healthcare settings alongside timetabled teaching sessions. Twelve clinical rotations across: Women's Health, Child Health, Mental Health, Community, Advanced Clinical Skills, Surgery, Emergency Department Medicine, General Practice, a Selective in a chosen sub-specialty area, and two Elective/pre-internship rotations undertaken in Australia or overseas. Assessment combines in-training assessment throughout the year with end-of-year written exams and Objective Structured Clinical Examinations (OSCEs). Students complete an MD project - a research-based project, a capstone experience, or a professionally focused project - culminating in a final report and presentation, plus a portfolio of work submitted at year end.
admission_requirements: Entry to the Doctor of Medicine follows successful completion of the Bachelor of Medical Studies within the Bond Medical Program. Direct entry to the combined program is limited to Australian citizens, Australian permanent residents, Australian Humanitarian visa holders and New Zealand citizens; international students can join via a recognised Bond pathway degree (Bachelor of Biomedical Science in the pre-health professional major, Master of Occupational Therapy, Doctor of Physiotherapy, Master of Nutrition and Dietetic Practice, or Master of Healthcare Innovations) provided they meet the required GPA and prerequisites for entry to Year 2 of the Medical Program.
english_requirements: English proficiency is met through the QCAA English-subject prerequisite (or a recognised equivalent) required for entry to the Bond Medical Program, reflecting the program's domestic-only direct-entry policy for Australian and New Zealand citizens and permanent residents.

name: Doctor of Philosophy
description: Bond's research doctorate, normally three to four years of full-time candidature across any of the university's faculties, including law, health sciences, business, communication and creative media. Admission is by research proposal plus a principal and associate supervisors, with a confirmation panel at the end of year one and regular progress reviews after that. The degree ends in a dissertation of about 80,000 to 100,000 words, or an equivalent creative work with exegesis in arts disciplines. Bond runs a dedicated Higher Degree by Research unit and emphasises a small, collegiate cohort with access to facilities such as Bloomberg terminals, production studios and clinical labs, conference funding, and paid tutoring opportunities. It suits people with a strong honours or master's background aiming at academic or advanced research careers.
curriculum: Thesis: The Doctor of Philosophy Thesis will be a major, substantially original, theoretical or empirical study of an issue pertaining to the student’s major field of study. Depending on the field of specialisation, the degree culminates in an 80,000-word thesis. Prior to formal application, applicants need to consider the specific research topic they wish to investigate and develop a thesis proposal in consultation with a potential supervisor. Thesis for Doctor of Philosophy The subject develops independent research skills and the ability to relate a specific research topic to a broad framework of knowledge. The program places a major emphasis on independent inquiry, a thorough understanding of domain specific knowledge, competence in research methodologies and on the ability to communicate research results. You are required to submit a substantial thesis, which is a significant and original contribution to the knowledge or understanding of your chosen Field of Research.
admission_requirements: Applicants should normally have a first degree with major studies in a relevant subject area, from a recognised institution, with a GPA of at least 75% in a major study area.

name: Doctor of Physiotherapy
description:
Bond's Doctor of Physiotherapy is accredited as an entry-level program by the Australian Physiotherapy Council and approved by the Physiotherapy Board of Australia, and it's built around problem- and case-based learning rather than a lecture-heavy model: each teaching block centres on clinical cases students work through in small groups, mirroring how physiotherapists actually reason through a patient in front of them.

The degree includes up to 1,400 hours of clinical placement, spread across genuinely different settings: acute care such as cardiorespiratory and orthopaedic wards, inpatient and outpatient rehabilitation, musculoskeletal outpatient clinics, and, depending on availability and student interest, paediatrics, women's and men's health, elite sports, and rural, remote or international placements. Bond also runs an on-campus community physiotherapy clinic, so some placement hours happen without students leaving the Gold Coast campus. The final semester is built around a clinical internship placement specifically designed to push students beyond the caseload variety they've already encountered, ahead of entering the profession.
curriculum:
Foundational trimesters: Musculoskeletal Physiotherapy, Cardiorespiratory Physiotherapy, Neurological Physiotherapy, Clinical Reasoning and Case-Based Learning
Clinical placement blocks (up to 1,400 hours total) across acute care, inpatient/outpatient rehabilitation, and musculoskeletal outpatient settings
Elective clinical placements (availability-dependent): paediatrics, women's/men's health, elite sports, rural, remote or international placement
On-campus community physiotherapy clinic placement
Final semester: clinical internship placement extending beyond core clinical experiences
Program accredited by the Australian Physiotherapy Council; approved by the Physiotherapy Board of Australia
admission_requirements: A completed bachelor's degree (health/science background preferred) with a competitive GPA; interview and/or additional selection criteria may apply.
english_requirements: IELTS Overall 7.0, with no band below 7.0 (registration-board English requirement).

name: Juris Doctor
description:
The Juris Doctor is Bond's graduate-entry law degree for students who already hold an undergraduate qualification in any discipline and want to qualify for legal practice without repeating an LLB. The program is built on 240 credit points, and most students take four subjects a trimester, which at Bond's three-trimester pace typically brings the degree in at around two years rather than the three years a JD usually takes elsewhere.

Students complete a compulsory core of foundational law subjects, including constitutional law, contracts and criminal law, then select 70 credit points of electives, with the option to complete a formal Law Specialisation by taking at least four electives (40 credit points) within one subject area. Practical legal skills are woven through the degree rather than taught separately: legal writing, oral communication, negotiation, dispute resolution and professional ethics all sit inside the JD's integrated skills and professionalism strand. Graduates who also want to complete practical training requirements can continue directly into Bond's Graduate Diploma in Legal Practice, meaning the whole path to admission as a legal practitioner can be finished at the one university.
curriculum:
Core subjects: Constitutional Law, Contract Law, Criminal Law and Procedure, Torts, Property Law, Equity, Administrative Law, Corporations Law, Evidence, Civil Dispute Resolution
Electives (70CP): drawn broadly across commercial, criminal, international and public law subjects
Optional Law Specialisation: minimum 4 electives (40CP) concentrated in one recognised specialisation area
Integrated skills and professionalism program: legal writing and reasoning, oral advocacy, negotiation, dispute resolution, professional ethics, embedded across trimesters
Total: 240 credit points, typically 4 subjects per trimester
Optional progression: Graduate Diploma in Legal Practice (GDLP) for practical training requirements toward admission
admission_requirements: A completed bachelor's degree in any discipline (does not need to be in law) with a competitive GPA.

Teaching is delivered through weekly live seminars plus recorded material and an AI tutor, with year one covering the foundational law subjects and electives and year two finishing the prescribed curriculum and a 15-day legal work experience placement.

That placement can count toward the workplace experience component of the Graduate Diploma in Legal Practice, which students typically take alongside or after the JD to complete the practical training required for admission. Applicants should confirm current entry requirements and, importantly, how the online JD is treated by the admitting authority in the state where they intend to practise, since admission rules are set by each jurisdiction.

description:
The longer of Bond's two actuarial master's degrees, six semesters (two years) at three subjects a semester, built for students without a related undergraduate background. The first four semesters mirror the Master of Actuarial Science content, from financial mathematics and mathematical statistics through stochastic processes, corporate finance and asset-liability modelling; the final two semesters add the Actuarial Control Cycle, data analytics and an actuarial research essay.

It suits people who enjoy mathematics and want the fullest set of professional exemptions from a single coursework degree, heading toward insurance, superannuation, risk or actuarial consulting.

name: Master of Business Administration
description:
Bond was Australia's first university to run a genuine three-semester-a-year academic calendar, and the MBA is where that timetable shows up most sharply: the full 12-subject generalist program can be completed in one year and four months of continuous study, roughly half the time a traditional two-semester MBA takes to deliver a comparable subject load. The first trimester front-loads eight core functional subjects delivered as intensive-mode bootcamps (compressed, immersive blocks rather than subjects spread thin across a normal semester) before students move into a business engineering component and then electives where they can build a specialisation.

Because Bond charges the same tuition to domestic and international students, cohorts are unusually mixed for an Australian MBA, and the accelerated calendar tends to attract candidates who want to return to the workforce, or start a venture, without a multi-year career gap. Students who want workplace exposure alongside the degree can take the MBA (Professional) variant, which follows the same subject structure with an additional 20-week professional placement component built in.
curriculum:
Trimester 1: 8 core functional bootcamps delivered in intensive mode (Accounting, Finance, Marketing, Economics, Organisational Behaviour, Operations, Strategy, Business Analytics)
Trimester 2: Business engineering component — integrated, project-based subjects connecting the core disciplines
Trimester 3: Electives, including the option to build a specialisation, plus a capstone strategy project
Optional MBA (Professional) pathway: same 12-subject structure plus an additional 20-week supervised professional placement

name: Master of Finance
description:
Bond's Master of Finance has been accepted into the CFA Institute University Affiliation Program, meaning the curriculum is deliberately mapped against the CFA Program Candidate Body of Knowledge rather than following a generic finance syllabus, useful for students planning to sit the CFA exams alongside or after the degree. It's designed for graduates from other disciplines who want a quantitatively rigorous route into financial markets, risk management and investment analysis, and runs across Bond's three trimesters to be completed in one year and four months.

Teaching is case-based and delivered with input from industry guest lecturers, and students get access to Bond's two financial trading rooms and 40 Bloomberg terminals, more Bloomberg terminals than any other Australian university offers, which matters for a degree built around live market data rather than textbook problem sets. Group projects and case presentations run throughout, so students graduate having actually built and defended investment analysis rather than only having studied the theory behind it.

A two-year degree (six semesters) that qualifies graduates for Dietitians Australia's Accredited Practising Dietitian program, the credential needed to work as a dietitian in Australia. name: Master of Project Management
description:
Bond is the only Australian university whose project management programs carry recognition from all three major industry bodies at once: the Australian Institute of Project Management, the Project Management Institute's Global Accreditation Center, and the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors. That's a fairly unusual claim to be able to make and shapes how the Master of Project Management is built. Rather than teaching a single methodology, the curriculum aligns to the PMBOK Guide while explicitly training students in predictive, adaptive and hybrid ways of working, since that's closer to how project teams actually operate outside a textbook.

The degree is organised around four study themes (strategy; sustainability; managing complex problems and teams; and virtual teams and global working) that recur across subjects rather than being confined to one unit each. Content covers conflict resolution, integrated planning, portfolio management, and both public- and private-sector investment and risk, and the degree can be completed across Bond's three trimesters faster than an equivalent two-semester program elsewhere.
